name: Black pill ideology

lead: The black pill is a worldview from online incel forums holding that dating and social success are determined largely by physical traits such as height and facial structure, and that unattractive men cannot escape this hierarchy. The name plays on the red pill and blue pill from The Matrix.

In looksmaxxing spaces it is a contested idea. Some users treat it as a motivation to optimise appearance, others as a source of despair, and some argue it undermines the self-improvement the subculture claims to offer. Academic research studies it mostly as part of incel ideology and its mental-health and violence-related correlates.

paras: The belief rests on claims about evolved mate preferences, hypergamy and selected dating-site statistics. Researchers describe forum members using technology and data to argue that attraction is biologically determined, and some psychologists have proposed frameworks linking such narratives to rejection sensitivity, grievance and identity fusion.

Research on incel communities reports high rates of depression, suicidality and social isolation among members, and a minority endorsement of violence against women. A 2022 survey cited by Wikipedia found most self-identified incels rejected violence. Anyone in distress can contact local crisis services.

lead: The black pill is a belief system associated with online incel (involuntary celibate) communities. Wikipedia describes it as a more nihilistic offshoot of the red pill idea, holding that dating and society mainly benefit women and physically attractive men and that unattractive men cannot escape this hierarchy because success is set by genetics.[1] The pill metaphor comes from The Matrix.[1]

In looksmaxxing, Wikipedia says the practice was coined on incel message boards in the 2010s and by the mid-2020s was more commonly linked with black pill ideology; the black pill is defined there as the belief that women's attraction depends mainly on physical traits like height and facial features.[2] Many looksmaxxers dispute that the idea implies giving up, and threads debate whether blackpill thinking helps or harms self-improvement.[3]

Academics study the black pill within research on incels, misogynistic extremism and mental health. A 2021 qualitative analysis of 9,062 comments on an incel forum found that members argue emerging technologies reveal and compound gender practices that produce involuntary celibacy.[4] A 2024 study found identity fusion with the incel ingroup predicted endorsement of violence against women.[5]
infobox: Looks and genetics largely determine romantic and social outcomes
The Matrix red pill and blue pill metaphor

paras: According to Wikipedia, proponents say women are hardwired to prefer a narrow set of masculine traits, a notion called hypergamy, and cite an 80/20 rule in which 80 percent of women are said to want the top 20 percent of men.[1] Collections of cited studies are called the scientific blackpill, and the Institute for Strategic Dialogue describes the use of this research as argument by exhaustion.[1]

Grokipedia describes the belief as often attributing 80 to 90 percent of outcomes to genetics and looks, and lists criticisms that it is deterministic, dismisses personality and behavior, and encourages fatalism.[6]

The term arose on incel forums. Wikipedia reports that the word incel itself was coined by a Toronto student in 1997 for an inclusive support project and later adopted by misogynistic forums, with Reddit banning r/incels in 2017 and r/braincels in 2019.[1] Looksmaxxing and the blackpill grew up alongside each other on PSL forums.[2]

A 2024 scoping review examined how misogynistic extremism is defined and reported conceptual confusion in the field.[7] A 2026 narrative review describes involuntary celibacy as a digital subculture that intersects with mental health burden and gender-based violence.[8] A 2025 study of 100 therapy discussion threads on a large incel forum noted high rates of depression, suicidality and social isolation and resistance to mental-health help.[9] A 2026 hypothesis article proposes a dual-pathways framework for incel mental health and ideology.[10]

Wikipedia reports that a 2022 study found 79 percent of surveyed self-identified incels rejected violence, and quotes researchers William Costello and David Buss suggesting extreme inceldom looks more like suicidality than violence toward others.[1]

No studies found testing the black pill's central claim as a clinical hypothesis. Related research on incel populations is observational and includes surveys, qualitative analyses and reviews of mental health and ideology.[4][5][8][9]

On looksmax.org, one thread argues that blackpill thinking has distorted what looksmaxxing originally was, a way to improve oneself, and that users give up over perceived flaws such as eye shape.[3] Other threads dispute whether the black pill is real. Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article says physicians and critics link the culture with body dysmorphia and suicidal ideation.[2]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org the black pill is both a founding premise and a point of contention.[3]
